segments.title: The Fog and What It Conceals

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the greatest novels in the English language.
Over the course of this series, we'll be living inside Dickens's most ambitious, most structurally daring, and — I would argue — most haunting work.
Bleak House was published in monthly instalments between 1852 and 1853, and it has never really gone away.
Today we begin at the beginning — with fog.
To help us unpack that opening, I'm joined by three people whose company I suspect Dickens himself would have enjoyed.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose scholarship on Dickens's craft is, frankly, the most exciting work in the field right now.
She reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — with love and with a magnifying glass.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has spent a lifetime defending Dickens against what he calls — and I think he means this affectionately — the ideological vultures.
For Edmund, Bleak House is above all a novel about character — about the moral weight individuals carry through an indifferent world.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt has read Bleak House five times and still finds new things on every page.
She is our reader's reader — the person at this table who reminds us what the novel feels like from the inside.
Now — fog.
The opening of Bleak House is one of the most audacious moves in Victorian fiction.
Dickens doesn't begin with a character, a plot, a house — he begins with weather.
Specifically, with fog — and the word itself is repeated something like twenty times in the first two pages.
It reads almost like an incantation.
The sentence structure does something extraordinary — it accumulates without resolving.
Dickens writes in this relentless present tense — "Fog everywhere. Fog up the river. Fog down the river."
"Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights."
It's not descriptive prose — it's a drumbeat.
And crucially, there is no narrator telling us how to feel about it.
We're simply in it — immersed before we've had a chance to get our bearings.
Eleanor is right about the rhythm, though I'd resist the temptation to over-allegorise the fog.
There is a tendency — a very modern tendency — to read the fog as capitalism, or the fog as bureaucracy, as if Dickens were writing a pamphlet.
He was not.
What the fog does, first and foremost, is establish atmosphere — a moral atmosphere, if you like.
The novel is saturated with obscurity — with things hidden, delayed, concealed.
And Dickens is telling us from the very first line that clarity — moral clarity, legal clarity — will be very hard to come by.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce itself is the great fog machine of the novel — a suit in Chancery so ancient that no living person can explain what it is actually about.
Dickens describes it as having, in its long sleep, "worn out" — and I'm paraphrasing — many a full-grown fool who had drifted into it from the beginning.
What strikes me every time I read that opening — and I've read it five times now, as you said — is how physical it feels.
You don't just understand the fog intellectually. You feel chilled by it.
And then Dickens lands this devastating image of the Lord High Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall at the heart of the fog.
He sets it up with such precision — let me try to give a sense of it.
"Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition of this High Court of Chancery."
"Groping and floundering" — those two words do so much work.
It's not just incompetent. It's helpless. It's almost pitiful.
And yet it destroys people. That tension is there from the very first chapter.
Caroline's point about physicality is crucial, and it connects to something structural I find endlessly fascinating.
Dickens is writing in the third person — this sweeping, almost godlike present-tense narrator — but very shortly he introduces Esther.
And Esther narrates her own story in the first person, past tense — warm, uncertain, intimate.
The structural effect is almost vertiginous — you move from the fog, which knows everything and judges everything, to a woman who keeps saying she doesn't know very much at all.
Esther's famous self-deprecation — "I know I am not clever" — is itself a kind of counter-fog.
She is the novel's attempt to see clearly — to find a human scale — inside an overwhelming obscurity.
I'm glad Eleanor has brought in Esther, because I think she is the moral centre of the novel — and she is perpetually underestimated by critics who find her too good to be interesting.
There is a kind of critical snobbery about goodness — as if virtue were inherently less novelistic than vice.
Dr. Johnson would have had something sharp to say about that.
What interests me about the fog in relation to Esther is what she cannot see — her own parentage, her own place in the world.
The fog is not merely meteorological or metaphysical — for Esther, it is personal.
She has been told from childhood that she is illegitimate, that her very birth is a shame — and she carries that obscurity into everything she does.
That moment early in Esther's narrative — when she speaks to her doll as a child, trying to understand what she has done wrong — it breaks my heart every reading.
Her godmother tells her it would have been better had she never been born — and Esther simply accepts it, internalises it.
Edmund, you're right that there's a snobbery about goodness.
But I think what Dickens is doing with Esther is showing how goodness is earned — painfully, quietly, in the dark.
She is the fog's opposite — not because she's cheerful, but because she chooses to see.
What I love about what's emerging here is that the fog is doing multiple things simultaneously — atmospheric, structural, moral, personal.
It's the novel's governing image — and we've barely left the first chapter.
In our next segment, we'll turn to Chancery itself — the fog made institutional — and ask what it does to the people trapped inside it.
Stay with us.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes one of the great Victorian novels apart — sentence by sentence, chapter by chapter — to see how it works and why it endures.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be reading Bleak House with three remarkable guides.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is frankly obsessed with how Dickens builds his effects — the architecture of a sentence, the weight of a single image.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who has spent a lifetime reading Dickens as a novelist of moral character rather than social polemic — and who is not afraid to say so.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times — which tells you something about this novel's hold on its readers.
Today we begin with what is, structurally speaking, the most audacious decision Dickens makes in the entire book: the dual narration.
Two voices, two temporal registers, two entirely different relationships to the reader — running in parallel for nine hundred pages.
Eleanor, let's start with you — what is Dickens actually doing when he splits the narration in two?
What he's doing is, in a word, scandalous — and I mean that as the highest praise.
In 1852, the novel as a form had conventions, and one of those conventions was that your narrator should at least be consistent.
Dickens throws that out entirely.
The novel opens with that famous anonymous voice — present tense, omniscient, almost hallucinatory — surveying London and Chancery with a kind of sardonic fury.
And then, without warning, in chapter three, we get Esther Summerson — past tense, first person, modest to the point of self-erasure.
The tonal whiplash is the point.
The anonymous narrator says, in that opening chapter, something like — the fog is everywhere, creeping up the river, creeping into the courts of Chancery.
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
That is a narrator who knows everything and trusts no one — including the reader.
Esther, by contrast, begins by telling us she is not clever, that she need not have said that, and then proceeds to be obviously, devastatingly clever for nine hundred pages.
The structural tension between those two voices is what holds the whole vast machine together.
Eleanor is quite right about the technical audacity, though I'd push back gently on the word machine.
Bleak House is not a mechanism — it is a moral universe, and the dual narration is how Dickens establishes its two poles.
The anonymous voice is judgment — cold, comprehensive, witheringly ironic.
Esther's voice is love — patient, particular, attending to persons rather than systems.
Burke wrote that society is a partnership between the living, the dead, and those yet to be born.
Dickens is doing something analogous: the omniscient narrator carries the dead weight of institutional failure, while Esther carries the living hope of moral renewal.
When Esther writes of her early childhood — shut away, made to feel she had no right to exist — the prose is searingly quiet.
"I had never heard my mama spoken of. I had never heard of my papa either."
That simplicity is not naivety — it is Dickens at his most disciplined, allowing the child's incomprehension to indict the adult world without a single editorial flourish.
What strikes me — and this is something I feel viscerally when I re-read — is how different the two narrators sound at the level of the sentence itself.
The anonymous narrator speaks in fragments, in rhetorical repetitions, in accumulating present-tense clauses that feel relentless.
Esther's sentences have a different rhythm entirely — they circle, they qualify, they double back.
There's a moment early on where she's trying to describe her feelings about Jarndyce's kindness, and she says something like —
"I felt so grateful to him, and admired him so much, and was so determined to be good enough to deserve his confidence."
Three clauses, each one adding a layer — gratitude, admiration, aspiration.
It's a syntax that enacts her character: always reaching, always qualifying, never quite satisfied with what she has already expressed.
And she does it while insisting she is not good at expressing herself.
The irony is so deep it has its own geology.
Caroline's point about syntax is exactly right, and I want to push it one step further.
The anonymous narrator operates in the eternal present — things are, not were.
Esther operates in the remembered past — she is always writing from a position of having survived, of looking back at suffering she has already endured.
This creates a structural irony that runs through the whole novel: we know Esther lives, because she is narrating.
But the anonymous chapters have no such safety net — anything can happen in the present tense, to anyone.
Think of the death of Krook — spontaneous combustion, rendered in that ferocious present-tense prose.
It is grotesque and sudden and impossible, and the present tense makes you feel like you cannot stop it.
The two narrators don't just tell different stories — they inhabit different relationships to time, and therefore to fate.
I find that account of temporal structure compelling, though I would frame the stakes somewhat differently.
The real question the dual narration poses is: which of these two worlds is more real?
The anonymous narrator's world — of institutions, fog, the grinding mill of Chancery — is vast and impersonal and seemingly inescapable.
But Esther's world — of friendship, of small kindnesses, of the particular face of a particular person — that world is also real, and Dickens insists upon its primacy.
Consider how she describes arriving at Bleak House for the first time — her wonder at the crooked staircases, the odd little rooms, the sense that the house itself is alive to her.
"I thought it was the most curious house that ever was seen."
Such a plain sentence, and yet it carries the whole weight of her capacity for wonder — wonder that has survived deprivation.
That is Dickens's argument: the personal, the loving, the particular — these are not diminished by the fog of institutions.
They are, in fact, the only answer to it.
Edmund's reading moves me, though I want to add something about the cost of being Esther's narrator.
Because there is a price Esther pays for her position in the narrative.
She cannot be an unreliable narrator in the conventional sense — her reliability is guaranteed by her goodness.
But that means she cannot fully see herself.
The moment I find most heartbreaking is when she picks up the mirror after her illness — after the smallpox has changed her face.
She writes — and this is so characteristic of her — that she was not shocked, that she had expected it, that she was prepared.
"I was very glad to find that I felt no particular emotion about it, certainly no grief."
But of course she is grieving — the whole rhythm of the prose gives it away.
Esther can narrate everything except her own suffering — which is perhaps the most devastating structural irony in the whole novel.
Yes — and this is where Dickens shows his deepest craft, because the anonymous narrator can see what Esther cannot.
The two narrations are not just structurally parallel — they are epistemically complementary.
Esther knows the texture of individual lives; the anonymous narrator knows the system that grinds those lives down.
Neither narrator alone can tell the whole story — which is, in itself, a kind of argument about the limits of any single perspective.
Dickens understood something that literary theorists would not put into formal language for another century: that narration is always partial, always positioned.
The only way to approach the whole truth is to triangulate between incompatible viewpoints.
That is what the dual narration does — and it does it with such apparent naturalness that you can read the whole novel without quite noticing the scaffolding.
That image of scaffolding feels exactly right — the invisible structure that holds a great building up.
What I'm hearing is that the dual narration is not a stylistic experiment Dickens tacked on — it is the novel's central argument in structural form.
Two kinds of knowledge, two kinds of truth, and the reader must hold them both simultaneously.
In our next segment, we'll move from how the novel is narrated to where it begins — that extraordinary opening, the fog, Chancery, the world before Esther arrives to humanise it.
Stay with us.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time with the novel's great structural mysteries — the fog, the Court, the slow grind of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
Now we turn to what I think is one of Dickens' most devastating portraits of a young man destroyed from within.
Richard Carstone — charming, gifted, fatally susceptible — and what the suit does to him.
Eleanor, you've written about Dickens' technique of showing character decline through accumulation rather than dramatic rupture — this seems the perfect case.
It's the perfect case, yes — and what makes it technically extraordinary is that Dickens never gives you a single scene you could point to and say: that is where Richard breaks.

The deterioration is woven into the fabric of Esther's narration — present in what she notices, what she tactfully omits, what she registers with that particular Esther sadness she can never quite suppress.
Think of how she describes him in the early chapters — he has this wonderful, buoyant energy, he tries everything, he can't fix on a profession.
And the reader laughs with him, almost — his restlessness is charming at first.
Dickens sets that charm up with great deliberateness, because he needs us to feel the loss.
You can't mourn the ruin of someone you never liked.
I'd agree with Eleanor on the technique — the gradual method is masterly.
But I would resist the temptation to make the suit the villain of the piece.
Richard's tragedy is, at its heart, a moral one — a failure of will, a refusal of the ordinary duties that constitute a life.
Jarndyce sees it with absolute clarity — and says so, repeatedly, with a generosity that Richard cannot receive.

There's a passage — one of the novel's most important, I think — where Jarndyce says to Esther something to the effect that the suit has made Richard its victim because Richard was first its willing prisoner.
That distinction between victimhood and complicity is the moral engine of Richard's story.
Burke would have recognised it — the man who surrenders his judgment to a chimera loses the capacity for genuine self-governance.
Edmund, I hear you on the moral architecture — but when I'm actually reading those scenes, what I feel most powerfully is pity.
Richard is so young.

And the novel keeps reminding you of that — there's that quality in Dickens' description of him where even as Richard grows haggard and suspicious, you can still glimpse the boy he was at Bleak House.
The scene that destroys me every time is near the end — when Ada is sitting with him and he says, in that exhausted, almost wondering way, 'I have been dreaming.'
'I have been dreaming.'
The simplicity of it — after everything, after all the schemes and the suspicions and the wasted years — that one line carries the whole tragedy.
Dickens earns that line by making us watch every step of the dream curdling.
Caroline's right that the deathbed language is devastating — and it works because of something structural that Dickens has set up much earlier.
The novel gives Richard a kind of double exposure throughout.
We see him through Esther's narration — and Esther loves him, so she softens, she qualifies, she hopes.
But then we also catch glimpses of him from the third-person narrator — and that narrator is far less forgiving.
The gap between those two views is itself a form of characterisation — we understand Richard better because we hold both pictures simultaneously.
That dual-narration architecture isn't just a formal experiment — it's load-bearing.
The craft point is well made — but I want to return to the question of what Richard actually loses, because I think it tends to be sentimentalised in modern readings.
What he loses is not merely happiness or health — he loses his honour.
He borrows money he cannot repay, he treats Jarndyce — his benefactor, a man of sterling character — with something approaching contempt.
He convinces himself that Jarndyce has a stake in preventing the suit's resolution — which is not merely wrong, it is ignoble.
Dickens is quite unsparing about this — he shows us Richard's rationalisation with a kind of clinical precision.
The great ghost of the suit, as Dickens puts it, has become the man's entire horizon.
The suspicion of Jarndyce — yes, that's the passage that breaks your heart, because you've seen how much Jarndyce has given.
And Dickens gives Jarndyce this extraordinary restraint in response — he never reproaches Richard directly.
He simply withdraws a little, and watches, and grieves.
Which is, in its own way, more damning than any confrontation would be.
There's a line Jarndyce has — something like: 'trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts' — and Richard can do neither.
He cannot trust in his own efforts because the suit has corroded the very faculty of effort.
That corrosion is the word — and Dickens makes it physical as well as moral.
By the later chapters Richard is described as gaunt, restless, living in mean lodgings near the Court — the geography of his life has contracted around the suit.
He haunts Chancery the way Krook haunts his rag-and-bottle shop — there's something of the same symbolic logic at work.
Both men are consumed by what they cannot let go of.
And Dickens presses the comparison further — Krook dies of spontaneous combustion, and Richard, we might say, dies of a kind of spontaneous moral combustion.
The novel is full of these dark structural rhymes — and Richard is one of its most resonant.
The Krook parallel is striking — though I suspect Dickens did not intend it quite so neatly.
But the deeper point stands.
What Richard's story gives us is something the Victorians understood rather better than we do — that a man's relationship to hope can become his greatest vulnerability.
Hope undisciplined by reason and exertion is merely appetite — and appetite, unchecked, consumes.
Johnson put it well when he wrote that the natural flights of the human mind are not from pleasure to pleasure, but from hope to hope.
Richard's flight from hope to hope is precisely what destroys him — each new profession, each new plan, is another hope he cannot sustain.
And what about Ada?
I always feel Ada is the novel's great unacknowledged grief — she loves Richard completely and she cannot save him, and she knows it.
Their secret marriage is both an act of devotion and a kind of surrender — Ada choosing to go down with him.
Esther is devastated when she finds out — and the scene where Ada tells her, with that quiet golden composure, is one of the most emotionally complex in the book.
Dickens gives Ada very little interiority — we rarely know what she truly thinks — and yet somehow her suffering is completely legible.
That is a very particular novelistic skill — making grief visible in a character who never articulates it.
Ada's silence is doing a great deal of work in that arc — yes.
And it throws Richard's volubility into sharp relief — he talks about the suit endlessly, he justifies, he theorises, he becomes almost monomaniacal in conversation.

There's a wonderful — if that's the right word — scene in the later chapters where even Vholes, the reptilian solicitor who feeds on Richard, seems momentarily uncomfortable at the intensity of his client's obsession.
Vholes, of course, is Richard's other great destroyer — the figure who represents the system's appetite for young men's futures.
Dickens describes him as cold, and black, and buttoned up — the imagery of a coffin lid is never far away.
The structural irony is perfect — Richard has invited his own undertaker to manage his affairs.
Vholes is one of Dickens' great satirical achievements — and yet I think the satire cuts in two directions.
Yes, Vholes is the system made flesh — cold, procedural, indefatigable.
But Vholes cannot operate without Richard's consent.
The solicitor has three daughters in Kennington and an aged father in the Vale of Taunton — Dickens gives him this grotesque family as a kind of moral deflection.
And Richard accepts it — accepts the idea that Vholes is a respectable man with dependants, and therefore safe.
That credulity is part of Richard's ruin — he is always willing to believe what he wishes to believe.
And that credulity is inseparable from the hopefulness Eleanor was describing at the start — it's the same quality, just darkened.
The boy who could turn his hand to anything, who took up the law and the army with equal brightness — that boy's openness has curdled into something that believes only what it needs to believe.
I re-read the final chapters recently and I was struck again by the physical detail Dickens gives us.
Richard's hand trembling, his eyes too bright — the body bearing witness to what the mind refuses to acknowledge.
When the suit finally collapses — consumed by costs — the news reaches Richard and for a moment he is almost peaceful.
As if the dream ending, even in catastrophe, is a kind of relief.
That moment of peace is so precisely observed — and it's followed immediately by collapse, which makes it unbearable.
What Dickens has understood — and this is the structural genius of it — is that Richard's life has been organised entirely around a future event.
Remove that event — even in failure — and the life has no remaining form.
There is nothing left to animate him.
It's one of the bleakest things in all of Victorian fiction — and it's done without melodrama, without a villain's speech, without any of the apparatus of sensation.
Just a young man, the dream gone, and the body following.
That phrase — the body following the dream — might be the most concise summary of Richard's arc I've heard.
What strikes me, listening to you all, is how much Richard functions as a kind of anti-Esther — his story running in dark parallel to hers throughout the novel.
Both wards of Jarndyce, both touched by the suit — but one sustains herself through smallness and service, and the other is destroyed by magnitude and expectation.
We'll take that thread into our next segment — what the novel makes of goodness under pressure, and whether Esther's particular goodness is triumph or compromise.

segments.title: The Blighted Child: Jo and the Cost of Injustice

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been working our way through the novel's great system of injustice — the Court of Chancery, the fog, the endless deferral of justice.
But no character pays a higher price for that system than Jo — the crossing-sweeper, the boy who knows nothing and is taught nothing and is swept away like so much London mud.
This segment is about Jo: what he represents, how Dickens constructs him, and why his death remains one of the most devastating moments in Victorian fiction.
Eleanor, you've written about Dickens's technique with marginal characters — Jo feels anything but marginal by the end.
Jo is one of the great structural miracles of the novel, I think.
He appears early — sweeping a crossing near Tom-all-Alone's — and Dickens is very deliberate about how little he is allowed to know.
The famous refrain — 'he don't know nothink' — is repeated with a kind of terrible insistence.
"He don't know nothink" — Dickens keeps returning to that phrase, and each time it lands differently.
At first it reads as ignorance; by the end it reads as indictment — of every institution that refused to teach him.
Dickens is constructing a cumulative argument — not a speech, not a pamphlet, but a living boy — and when you finally understand what that argument is, it's almost unbearable.
The craft is hiding in plain sight.
I'd agree with Eleanor that Jo is structurally indispensable — though I'd resist reading him purely as a sociological exhibit.
What moves me about Jo is his moral clarity — or rather, the moral clarity of those around him compared to their own pretensions.
He cannot read, he cannot pray in any formal sense — and yet when he is asked to show Inspector Bucket where Nemo is buried, he removes his hat.
That gesture is worth a thousand of Mr. Chadband's sermons.
And consider what Dickens does with Jo and Esther when she asks him to guide her to the burial ground.
"He don't know her. He has never seen her. But somehow a link is formed between them."
Dickens is doing something very delicate there — suggesting that goodness recognises goodness across every social barrier.
That is not a political argument. That is a moral one.
What always undoes me is the passage where Dickens speaks directly to the reader about Jo.
He breaks from the narrative entirely and addresses us — almost accusingly.
He sets it up so quietly, and then he turns on you.
"Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order."
"Dead, men and women, born with Heavenly compassion in your hearts. And dying thus around us every day."
I cannot read that without stopping.
Every time.
That list — Majesty, lords, Right Reverends, Wrong Reverends — it's the whole hierarchy of England skewered in four lines.
And notice what Dickens does architecturally in that passage — the anaphora, the repetition of 'Dead.'
It's a funeral oration and an indictment simultaneously.
The form performs the content — the repetition is itself a kind of knocking on a door that nobody will open.
And it's worth remembering that Jo has already been 'moved on' throughout the novel — by the police, by Tulkinghorn's agents, by Bucket himself.
He is never allowed to stay anywhere. The city is simply not made for him.
So his death is the logical conclusion of a life spent being told: not here, not now, not you.
Eleanor is right that the 'moving on' is central — but I'd frame it differently.
The policeman who moves Jo on is not the villain of the piece — he is himself trapped in a system he did not design.
Dickens understands this — that institutional cruelty operates through ordinary men following ordinary rules.
Burke would have called it the tyranny of precedent — the accumulated deadweight of unchallenged habit.
What Dickens adds — and this is his genius — is a face. A specific, grimy, bewildered, unknowing face.
And when the light goes out in that face, the argument is complete without a word of editorial commentary.
There's a moment just before Jo dies — when Allan Woodcourt is with him — that I find almost impossible to get through aloud.
Allan tries to teach Jo the Lord's Prayer. Jo has never heard it.
He tries to repeat the words — and Dickens writes it out, this halting, fragmentary attempt.
"'Our Father' — says Jo. 'Our Father' — very good, sir.'"
He is trying to please. Even now, dying, he is trying to give the right answer to the person attending him.
And then he stops. And the chapter ends.
Dickens doesn't describe the death. He doesn't need to.
That restraint is everything, isn't it.
Dickens, who is often accused of excess — of sentiment laid on too thick — chooses at the crucial moment to show almost nothing.
Jo stops in mid-prayer and Dickens pivots immediately to that savage address to the reader.
The effect is a kind of whiplash — tenderness into fury within a single paragraph.
That juxtaposition is the argument. You cannot separate them.
Jo connects to so much else in this novel — Esther's illness, Tom-all-Alone's, Lady Dedlock's secret journey.
Edmund, does Jo's function in the plot ever risk reducing him to a device — a vector, almost, for the novel's themes?
It's a fair challenge — and Dickens is not entirely innocent of that charge.
Jo is the linchpin of the plot — it is his inadvertent guidance of the disguised Hortense, and then Lady Dedlock, that sets the catastrophe in motion.
He carries smallpox from Tom-all-Alone's into Bleak House, infecting Charley and through Charley, Esther.
So yes — he is a narrative mechanism as well as a human being.
But I think the question is whether he transcends the mechanism — and I believe he does, precisely because Dickens gives him a specific relationship with Nemo.
Jo is perhaps the only person in London who mourns Nemo without any ulterior motive.
His loyalty to a dead man who was kind to him once — that is a moral fact that no plot function can exhaust.
That relationship with Nemo is so important — because Nemo is the only adult who ever treated Jo as a human being rather than an obstruction.
And Jo repays that with a faithfulness that shames everyone else in the novel.
When he is asked about the man — this nameless, penniless, dead law-writer — Jo says he was 'wery good to me, he wos.'
"He wos wery good to me, he wos."
That's all. Four words of imperfect grammar. And it's the most eloquent eulogy in the book.
Dickens understood that the most moving things are often said by people who don't have the words for them.
There's another formal dimension worth noting — Jo is one of the few characters who belongs entirely to the third-person narrator.
Esther's first-person narration never directly encompasses him — he exists in the other half of the novel's doubled vision.
And the omniscient narrator — Dickens's most sarcastic, most outraged voice — claims him.
It's as if Esther's warmth is too delicate an instrument for the scale of Jo's suffering.
You need the other voice — the voice that can be furious, that can address the Queen directly — to do justice to what happened to him.
Jo, then, as the novel's conscience — and the point where its two narratives converge into a single moral claim.
What strikes me, hearing all three of you, is that Jo works because Dickens refuses to let him be abstract.
The broom, the crossing, the particular sound of his dialect — it's all very precise.
When we come back, we're turning to Esther Summerson — the narrator who, in some ways, is Jo's mirror image: the child who was taken in, rather than the child who was cast out.

segments.title: Secrets and Surveillance: Lady Dedlock's Game

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time in the fog of Chancery, and in the warm domesticity of Esther's narrative.
Now we turn to the figure who I think haunts the novel most powerfully from a distance — Lady Dedlock.
This segment is about secrets and surveillance — the way she is watched, and the way she watches herself.
Eleanor, you've written about the architecture of concealment in Victorian fiction — where does Lady Dedlock fit in that tradition?
She fits at the very apex of it, I think — and she does something no other Dickens character quite manages.
She carries the secret of Esther's birth through the entire novel like a stone in the chest, and yet she performs perfect aristocratic stillness at every moment.
Dickens introduces her in those early chapters with that devastating phrase about her being 'bored to death.'
'Bored to death.'
It sounds like social satire — and it is — but it's also a woman describing her own psychological condition.
The boredom is armour.
What she cannot feel safely, she refuses to feel at all.
I take your point about the armour, Eleanor, though I'd frame it rather differently.
What Dickens is doing with Lady Dedlock is fundamentally a study in the cost of pride — classical, almost Aristotelian in its structure.
She made one catastrophic moral choice in her youth and spent twenty years constructing an identity that could not accommodate its consequences.
Dickens gives us that extraordinary moment in chapter two when she catches sight of the handwriting on Jarndyce's legal papers — Hawdon's handwriting — and almost faints.
The past does not stay buried.
It never does, in Dickens.
And that is not a social argument — that is a moral one.
What strikes me every time I read those early chapters is just how much Dickens asks us to hold in suspension.
We see Lady Dedlock before we understand her.
And Dickens is so precise about what she shows the world — that magnificent, glacial composure.
He describes her as having 'that exhausted composure' — a woman who has arrived at stillness through exhaustion, not ease.
'That exhausted composure.'
Those two words together are heartbreaking once you know her story.
On re-reading, they land completely differently.
And surveillance is central to her predicament — she is perpetually watched.
Tulkinghorn watches her with extraordinary patience and menace.
Eleanor, how do you read Tulkinghorn as a structural presence in the novel?
Tulkinghorn is one of Dickens' greatest achievements, and I think underrated even now.
He functions as a kind of anti-narrator — he gathers information the way a novelist does, but he uses it for power rather than meaning.
He never acts rashly.
He simply — accumulates.
Dickens describes him as 'surrounded by a mysterious halo of family confidences' — the solicitor as keeper of secrets is almost a Gothic figure here.
'Surrounded by a mysterious halo of family confidences.'
What I love about that phrase is the word 'halo' — it's mock-sacred, it makes Tulkinghorn into a dark priest of private knowledge.
The dark priest is apt, yes — though I'd say what makes Tulkinghorn truly frightening is his complete indifference to human feeling.
He is not sadistic, he is simply incurious about suffering.
His interest in Lady Dedlock's secret is professional — even aesthetic, one might say.
He treats her humiliation as a case to be managed, not a person to be pitied or even punished in any passionate sense.
That, to me, is far more disturbing than malice.
There's a scene I keep returning to — when Tulkinghorn visits Lady Dedlock at Chesney Wold and essentially tells her that he knows.
And he doesn't accuse her.
He simply makes her understand that he has the power to destroy her, and then he leaves.
It's the most terrifying form of cruelty — the threat held permanently in reserve.
And her response is almost noble.
She gives him nothing.
No tears, no pleading.
Just that terrible composure, held intact by sheer will.
And this is where the dual narration becomes so important, structurally.
Esther never knows most of this is happening.
The third-person narrator tracks Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock with this cool, omniscient irony.
Esther, meanwhile, is living her small, tender, daily life — entirely unaware that her origins are being used as a weapon.
The irony is almost unbearable.
And Dickens withholds it from us just long enough that when the two narratives finally converge on the secret, the emotional impact is enormous.
I want to bring in the scene where Lady Dedlock goes to the pauper burial ground in disguise — dressed as a servant girl, seeking Hawdon's grave.
This, to me, is the moral heart of her character.
Whatever she has concealed, whatever pride she has armoured herself in, she still goes to him.
The gesture is an act of faithfulness — almost of contrition.
Dickens writes of 'that deserted, desecrated place' — the burial ground where the poor are thrown without ceremony.
'That deserted, desecrated place.'
The doubled adjective is an indictment — of a society that buries its inconvenient dead in conditions of squalor.
And yet Lady Dedlock goes there anyway.
That is character, not social programme.
It's one of the most moving things in the novel, I think.
She goes in disguise — which is itself a kind of metaphor for her entire life.
And the Jo connection is so important — it's the crossing of worlds that Dickens makes structurally central.
Jo, the crossing-sweeper who knew Captain Hawdon, becomes unwittingly the link between Lady Dedlock and her past.
And the way Dickens writes Jo's observation of this grand lady weeping at a pauper's grave — there's no sentimentality in it.
Just a child's bewilderment, which is more devastating than any commentary could be.
And then the surveillance closes in — Bucket is set on her trail.
Inspector Bucket is remarkable — he's the detective as another kind of all-seeing eye.
Where Tulkinghorn accumulates secrets for power, Bucket pursues truth — but the machinery of pursuit is just as relentless.
Dickens describes his forefinger as almost having a life of its own — pointing, gesturing, accusing.
The forefinger that is always noting, always watching.
By the end of the novel, Lady Dedlock has been watched from every angle — by Tulkinghorn, by Bucket, by Hortense — until she simply runs.
She can no longer perform the stillness.
Her flight and death are the novel's most tragic action — and Dickens earns every measure of it.
She is found dead at the gate of the burial ground — the very gate she first visited in disguise.
The symmetry is almost classical — she dies where she first allowed herself to feel.
And Esther's recognition of her — recognising her own features in the figure on the ground — is one of the great moments in all of English fiction.
Esther writes: 'I passed on to the gate, and she lay there amongst the mud and at the foot of the step.'
The mud. The step.
Dickens never over-explains.
I can barely read that scene without stopping.
What undoes me is Esther's voice in that moment — so careful, so controlled, while describing something utterly shattering.
It's as if Esther has inherited the composure she never knew was her mother's.
The secrecy has passed down — even in the way she writes about it.
That's Dickens at his most profound — when the form of the writing enacts the theme.
The secret survives even in the silence around it — that seems like the perfect note to carry forward.
Lady Dedlock — watched, armoured, and finally broken — remains one of the most complex figures Dickens ever drew.
After a short break, we'll turn to the other great secret keeper of Bleak House — the legal system itself, and the case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.

segments.title: Laughter in the Darkness: Dickens' Comic Voice

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time in the fog, in the Court of Chancery, in the long shadow of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
But Bleak House is also, and this sometimes surprises first-time readers, a very funny novel.
Dickens is playing both instruments at once — the comedy and the tragedy — and this segment is about how he does that, and why it matters.
Eleanor, you've written about Dickens' comic architecture — the way jokes are built into the structure of the prose itself.
Where do you want to start?
I want to start with Mrs. Jellyby, because she is one of the most precisely constructed comic characters in all of Victorian fiction.
The joke is immediate and devastating: here is a woman of boundless philanthropic energy, entirely devoted to the natives of Borrioboola-Gha, who cannot see the child tumbling down her own staircase.
But what makes it structurally brilliant is the way Dickens gives us that comedy through Esther's narration.
Esther is too kind to say directly that Mrs. Jellyby is a monster of neglect.
So she reports the facts with perfect wide-eyed neutrality, and the gap between what she says and what we understand is where the comedy lives.
Dickens is using Esther's goodness as a comic instrument — her inability to condemn generates the condemnation.
And Peepy — let's not forget Peepy, the child who is forever tumbling about and entirely ignored.
There's a particular sentence where Esther notices him wedged behind the coal scuttle, and she simply notes it, moves on.
The comedy is in the brevity — Dickens doesn't linger, and that restraint is funnier than any amount of elaboration.
But then there's Mr. Guppy, who is funny in an entirely different register — he's comic through his own self-importance.
His proposal of marriage to Esther in chapter nine is one of the funniest scenes in the novel.
He frames this declaration of love in the language of a legal brief — he sets out his circumstances, his prospects, his 'humble dwelling.'
'I reside at Penton Place, Pentonville. It is lowly, but airy, open at the back, and considered one of the 'ealthiest outlets.'
The dropped H on 'healthiest' does all the social comedy Dickens needs in a single syllable.
I find Guppy genuinely interesting because Dickens does not quite despise him — which would have been the easier, lazier choice.
There is something almost touching in the man's absolute confidence in his own eligibility.
One thinks of what Johnson said about second marriages — the triumph of hope over experience.
Guppy's hope is his defining characteristic, and Dickens is far too humane a moralist to make it merely ridiculous.
But the comedian I find most remarkable in this novel is Mr. Skimpole.
Because Skimpole is a joke that becomes an indictment — and one doesn't notice the transition until it is too late.
Skimpole is Dickens at his most dangerous — I think that's exactly right, Edmund.
He introduces himself as a child — he's famously a 'mere child in the world' — and that self-description is offered as pure charm.
'I am a child, you know! I don't mean literally a child — I mean in my transactions with the world.'
And on first encounter it is charming — Jarndyce is charmed, Esther is charmed, the reader is charmed.
But Dickens is engineering a very slow revelation: the child is a parasite, and his childishness is a choice.
By the time he hands Jo the constable's half-crown — betraying the boy for cash while humming about the loveliness of life — the comedy has curdled entirely.
That structural arc from enchanting rogue to moral horror is one of Dickens' greatest achievements in this novel.
What strikes me about the comic voice in this novel is how much work it does for grief.
Think of the Bagnet family — Mrs. Bagnet, who is clearly the military genius of the household, while old Bagnet insists that his wife must speak for herself.
It's consistently funny — Bagnet's rule that he never gives his own opinion, always channelling it through her — but it's also a portrait of a genuinely happy marriage.
And Dickens places that warmth right next to George's predicament and Gridley's fury — as if to say, human life contains all of this at once.
The comedy doesn't escape the darkness.
It just makes it bearable enough to stay in the room.
Quite so — and I think the figure who crystallises this most perfectly is Tony Jobling, known as Weevle.
He is in many ways a trivial character — Guppy's amiable but feckless companion — and yet Dickens lodges him in Krook's house for a purpose.
The scene in which the two young men keep vigil on the night of Krook's spontaneous combustion is — for most of its length — purely comic.
They chatter about nothing, they fuss about their supper, they are magnificently oblivious.
And then something greasy and offensive settles on the windowsill, and the comedy is extinguished — as Krook himself has been extinguished.
Dickens understood — as Shakespeare understood — that laughter makes horror more horrible, not less.
That Krook scene is a masterclass in tonal engineering.
There's also something I want to flag about Dickens' comic prose at the sentence level — the sheer musicality of how he builds a gag.
Take the third-person narrator on the opening of Chancery — it's black comedy of the highest order.
He describes the legal suitors as having their 'bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits' — and the list goes on and accelerates.
'Scores of persons have deliriously found themselves made parties in Jarndyce and Jarndyce without knowing how or why.'
'Deliriously' — that word is doing incredible comic work.
It's absurd and tragic at once — which is Dickens' entire method in miniature.
Absurd and tragic at once — I think that's the note to carry forward.
We've been talking about how Dickens uses comedy structurally, tonally, and at the level of the sentence itself.
And what's emerged is that in Bleak House, laughter is never an escape hatch — it's always load-bearing.

Coming up, we're going to look at what might be the novel's most controversial artistic choice — the decision to split the narrative voice between the omniscient third-person and Esther's intimate first-person.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Reading Esther's Goodness: The Difficulty of Virtue

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time with the fog, with Chancery, with the great satirical machinery Dickens sets in motion.
But now we turn to the novel's most contested, most intimate creation: Esther Summerson.
Esther narrates roughly half of Bleak House in the first person — which is itself an extraordinary structural gamble.
And she is, by design, conspicuously good — patient, selfless, industrious, endlessly attentive to others.
For some readers, that goodness is the beating heart of the novel.
For others, it is the one thing they cannot quite bring themselves to believe in.
Eleanor, Edmund, Caroline — you have all lived with this character for a long time.
I want to begin with a simple, almost unfair question: do you trust Esther?
Trust her — that's exactly the right word, and exactly the right difficulty.
The first thing Esther tells us about herself is that her godmother raised her to feel, essentially, that her birth was a kind of original sin.
And her response to that cruelty is to become useful — frantically, almost compulsively useful.
She says to herself, very early on, something I find devastating in its modesty.
"I would try, as hard as ever I could, to repair the fault I had been born with."
She calls her own existence a fault.
And yet she never seems bitter.
That combination — the wound absorbed so completely it becomes self-improvement — is what makes her both moving and, for some readers, slightly unnerving.
What Caroline is identifying is a kind of structural paradox at the heart of Esther's narration.
She is the narrator, so she controls what we see — and yet she consistently refuses to claim credit for what she does.
She deflects praise constantly.
The joke — and Dickens is quite deliberate about this — is that the more she denies her own virtues, the more the narrative proves them.
Think of the way she describes her housekeeping keys — she mentions them almost as a nervous habit, a tic of self-definition.
Those keys are doing extraordinary symbolic work.
She becomes Dame Durden, the little old woman — it's a persona she adopts to deflect emotion, to make herself manageable.
And I think the self-deprecating nicknames — Dame Durden, old woman, little Rick's guardian — are Dickens encoding the psychological damage right into her speech patterns.
The architecture of her sentences performs the self-erasure her upbringing demanded.
I want to pause on something, because I think we are in danger of being too clever about Esther.
The instinct to diagnose her goodness as a symptom — as damage, as compulsion — is very much a modern instinct.
Dickens, I believe, meant it as a moral achievement.
Dr. Johnson observed that the greatest virtues are those maintained in the face of the greatest discouragement.
Esther was told from childhood that she should not have been born.
And from that unpromising ground she cultivates — consciously, effortfully — gratitude, industry, and care for others.
That is not pathology.
That is character.
When she nurses Jo, when she sits with Richard in his decline, she is not performing virtue — she is simply being it.
Edmund is right that it would be a reduction to call her merely damaged.
But I think the difficulty for readers — particularly modern readers — is the way she tells her own story.
She is incapable of saying plainly: I did this, and I was right to do it.
Take the smallpox episode — one of the most harrowing sequences in the novel.
She contracts the disease from Jo, and she nearly dies.
And when she wakes and looks in the mirror and sees that her face is changed forever — Dickens gives her this extraordinary, utterly characteristic response.
"I was very much changed — I knew I was — but I felt thankful to be alive."
Thankful to be alive.
Not angry.
Not despairing.
I find that almost unbearably moving — and also, if I'm honest, almost unbearably difficult to fully accept.
That moment is where I think Dickens is doing something technically very bold.
We have two narrative strands in this novel — Esther's first person, and the third-person omniscient narrator.
The omniscient narrator is savage, ironic, merciless — the narrator of Chancery and Krook and Mrs. Jellyby.
But Esther's narration has an entirely different texture — warmer, slower, full of what you might call compassionate noticing.
I think the dual narration is itself a moral argument.
The world without Esther's perspective is brilliant but pitiless.
Dickens is saying: you need both kinds of vision to see the whole picture.
The satirist who tears the world apart, and the woman who — quietly, stubbornly — holds it together.
Eleanor's point about the dual narration is well made, and I'd press it one step further.
The omniscient narrator can expose Sir Leicester Dedlock, can anatomise Harold Skimpole, can reduce Chadband to a grease-spot of hypocrisy.
But that narrator cannot tell us what it feels like to love Richard Carstone when he is destroying himself.
Only Esther can do that.
She sits with him near the end — she has gone to find him in his lodgings, he is pale and shrunken with disappointment — and she holds on to kindness when every fact argues against it.
Dickens gives her a phrase I think about often.
"I sat down by him and told him that we counted on his being well and strong before another winter came."
She knows it is almost certainly not true.
But she says it — because hope offered with full knowledge of the odds against it is not self-deception.
It is, I would argue, the highest form of kindness.
And then he dies.
That's the thing that always lands on me like a weight.
Esther's goodness doesn't save Richard.
It doesn't save Jo.
Chancery grinds on regardless.
And I think Dickens knows this is the genuine difficulty of virtue — that it doesn't guarantee outcomes.
Esther cannot dismantle the system.
What she can do — and what Dickens insists is worth everything — is remain fully present to the person in front of her.
That's beautifully put, and it connects to something about the ending that I always want to argue about.
Esther ends the novel married to Woodcourt, happy, in a new Bleak House — and some readers find that saccharine, a reward too neatly given.
But look at the last sentence of the whole novel — Esther stops herself mid-thought.
She starts to say that she is not as pretty as she was, and then she won't finish the sentence.
"And I have been too happy — and am now, to think of such things."
That dash — that refusal to complete the thought about her changed face — is Dickens being a very subtle craftsman.
The wound is still there.
The happiness is real.
And Esther, true to herself to the last, moves on before she lets us see her grieve.
That closing dash is, I think, one of the most perfect endings in Victorian fiction.
Not triumphant.
Not resolved.
Simply — still going.
Esther Summerson is a woman who was told her existence was an error and who chose — every single day, in the smallest acts — to insist otherwise.
That is the difficulty of virtue Dickens is writing about.
Not its grand occasions — but its daily, unwitnessed, uncelebrated practice.
Dame Durden — unwitnessed, uncelebrated, and yet somehow the moral centre of the largest novel in the English language.
After the break, we'll turn to the legal world she moves through — Chancery, Tulkinghorn, and the question of who really holds power in this novel.

segments.title: The Labyrinth Resolved: What Bleak House Teaches

utterances.text: We've spent this episode inside the fog, the lawsuits, the secrets, and the suffering that make Bleak House one of the great moral architectures in English fiction.
Now, as we reach the novel's end, the question we want to sit with is this: what does Bleak House actually teach us?
Not what it argues about the law, or about class, or about Victorian England — but what it leaves in the reader's bones.
Eleanor, you've been thinking about the architecture of the whole novel. What does the ending — Esther's ending — resolve, and what does it deliberately leave open?
What strikes me most about the ending is that Dickens gives us two endings — structurally, formally — and neither one fully closes.
The third-person narrator, that omniscient cold eye, simply stops — Chancery is done, Jarndyce and Jarndyce has consumed itself, the estate entirely eaten up in costs.
And then Esther's narrative continues, and it's warm, domestic, small — deliberately small.
She has a new Bleak House, she has Woodcourt, she has her children — and yet she can't quite finish her own sentence.
She says — and this is the last line of the novel — something like: 'I know that my face is not the face it was, and yet I have been told it is prettier still.'
'I have been told that it is prettier still.'
She won't say it herself. She can't claim her own loveliness. Even in happiness, Esther is still deflecting.
That's a structural choice of breathtaking precision — Dickens ends on a sentence that is grammatically incomplete, emotionally unresolved, and perfectly true to character.
Eleanor is right about the structural doubleness, and I think it illuminates something that critics who read this novel primarily as social critique often miss.
The fog lifts. Chancery collapses. But what Dickens insists upon is that the true drama was never institutional — it was moral.
Richard Carstone is not destroyed by the Court of Chancery. He is destroyed by the weakness of his own will, his inability to anchor himself to any honest purpose.
Dickens is quite explicit: Richard cannot fix himself, because he will not fix himself.
The novel teaches, as Burke might have said, that institutions do not corrupt men — corrupted men corrupt institutions.
And set against Richard's dissolution, we have Jarndyce — a man who, having learned what the suit cost his great-uncle, simply refuses to let it cost him his soul.
Dickens gives Jarndyce the most quietly heroic act in the novel — releasing Esther from their engagement — and he does it without complaint, without claim, without a word of self-pity.
That, I would submit, is what Bleak House teaches above all: that goodness is possible, and that it asks everything.
I find myself agreeing with both of you, and wanting to add something that comes from the experience of finishing the novel rather than analysing it.
Because every time I reach the end — and I've read it five times now — I feel a particular pang that I think Dickens engineered deliberately.
Jo the crossing-sweeper dies in the middle of the novel — not at the end, not in a climactic chapter, but quietly, surrounded by people trying to help him, and it is too late.
And Dickens steps out of the fiction to address the reader directly. He says — and I have this more or less by heart —
'Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right reverends and wrong reverends of every order. Dead, men and women, born with heavenly compassion in your hearts.'
It's one of the most devastating passages in the Victorian novel. He's not addressing his characters. He's addressing us.
And that, for me, is the lesson Bleak House insists on more urgently than any other: that the fog is not just outside. It is what we permit.
That passage about Jo — the 'Dead, your Majesty' — is one of those moments where Dickens just abandons the pretence of fiction entirely.
And structurally, it's fascinating — because Esther's narration never does that. Esther never breaks the fourth wall.
The third-person narrator carries the anger, the indictment, the rhetoric. Esther carries the feeling.
So the dual narration isn't just a stylistic experiment — it's a moral division of labour.
The novel teaches us — through its very form — that you need both: the political indignation and the personal tenderness.
Neither alone is sufficient. That is an extraordinarily sophisticated thing for a novel to argue through its architecture rather than its plot.
I shall concede Eleanor's point about the architecture — one must concede what is plainly true — and yet I want to press on one thing.
The novel's final image of possibility is not institutional reform. It is Esther's new Bleak House — a home, maintained with love, in spite of everything.
Dickens spent his life reforming, campaigning, satirising — and yet when he imagines salvation, he imagines it at the domestic scale.

Miss Flite, that lovely broken figure, has waited decades for the judgment that never comes — and her caged birds, which she names things like Hope and Youth and Beauty and Despair, are the novel's most sustained image.
At the end, she releases them. And that release — tiny, private, symbolic — is offered as something real.
Not a revolution. A release. Dickens, in the end, is a novelist of the possible — and the possible is always small, always human, always particular.
Miss Flite's birds. I think about them every time.

She names them — Hope, Joy, Youth, Peace, Rest, Life, Dust, Ashes, Waste, Want, Ruin, Despair, Madness, Death, Cunning, Folly, Words, Wigs, Rags, Sheepskin, Plunder, Precedent, Jargon, Gammon, and Spinach.
Dickens hid the joke right there in the list — Gammon and Spinach — slang for nonsense. In the middle of the elegy, there's the comedian.
That's what I keep coming back to, as a reader: Bleak House is very funny. Persistently, uncomfortably funny.
Guppy's absurd proposals to Esther. Turveydrop's monstrous vanity. Mr. Chadband's oily rhetoric.
The comedy is not ornament. It is Dickens saying: this is how human beings actually behave — vain, ridiculous, self-deceiving — and we must see that clearly if we are to love them honestly.
That is what Bleak House teaches me, re-reading after re-reading: see clearly, love honestly, and do not wait for the judgment.
See clearly, love honestly, and do not wait for the judgment. I can't imagine a better note on which to end.
Bleak House is a novel that asks its readers to hold two things at once: righteous anger at a world arranged to grind people down, and a stubborn tenderness for the people being ground.
Eleanor, Edmund, Caroline — you've made a very long and very great novel feel alive and necessary this hour. Thank you.
For our listeners: if you haven't read Bleak House, we hope we've given you a reason to begin. If you have, we hope we've given you a reason to go back.
Either way, the fog is waiting — and so, we promise, is the light.
